summary: The note traces the history and structure of the states (Länder) of Germany. It covers the origin of the term Länder in the Weimar Constitution of 1919, the failed and limited efforts to redraw state boundaries, and the district system (Kreise) used within states. It also summarizes Germany's federal tradition from the Holy Roman Empire through the German Confederation and Empire to the Nazi-era abolition of effective state autonomy.
one_line: Overview of the history, naming, boundary changes, and district structure of Germany's federal states from the Weimar era onward.
key_facts: The term Länder (Lands) dates back to the Weimar Constitution of 1919; before this the constituent states of the German Empire were called Staaten (States).
The term Bundesland is very common today but is not used officially, neither by the 1919 constitution nor by the Basic Law of 1949.
Bavaria (since 1919), Saxony (originally since 1919 and again since 1990), and Thuringia (since 1994) call themselves Freistaaten (Free States).
Hugo Preuss, the father of the Weimar Constitution, drafted a plan to divide the German Reich into 14 roughly equal-sized states, which was turned down.
Article 18 of the Weimar Constitution required three fifths of the votes handed in, and at least the majority of the population, to decide on a territorial alteration.
Before 1933 there were only four changes in the configuration of the German states, including the merger of the 7 Thuringian states in 1920.
Pyrmont joined Prussia in 1922, and Waldeck did so in 1929.
Every German state except the city-states of Berlin, Hamburg, and Bremen consists of Landkreise (rural districts), Kreisfreie Städte, or Kommunalverbände besonderer Art.
The Holy Roman Empire comprised more than 300 petty states around 1796.
After the Congress of Vienna (1815), 39 states formed the German Confederation.
The new German Empire included 25 states (three of them Hanseatic cities) and the imperial territory of Alsace-Lorraine.
Prussia controlled 65% of the territory and 62% of the population of the German Empire.
The remaining states were gradually de facto abolished and reduced to provinces under the Nazi regime via the Gleichschaltung process.
The states administratively were largely superseded by the Nazi Gau system.
